chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Hanan ibn Sadeer who said:

We entered upon Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) and with us was Farqad the cupper. He said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I perform a work and I have asked about it more than one and not just two, and they claimed that it is a disliked work, and I love to ask you about it. If it is disliked, I will refrain from it and perform other works, for I will end up in that according to your word.' He said, 'What is it?' He said, 'Cupping.'

He said, 'Eat from your earnings, O cousin, and give in charity, and perform Hajj from it, and marry, for the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) had cupping done and gave the wage, and if it were forbidden, he would not have given it.'

He said, 'May Allah make me your ransom, I have a male goat which I hire out, so what do you say regarding its earnings?' So he said, 'Eat its earnings, for it is permissible for you, and the people dislike it.'
Hanan said, 'I said, For what reason do they dislike it and it is permissible?' He said, 'For the people reproaching one another (for that work).'

key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: Disliked (less than haram, but not preferred)

ai.seo_question: Is the earnings of a cupper halal or haram in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between legal permissibility (*halal*) and social preference (*makruh*), clarifying that the public's aversion to cuppers' earnings stems from social reproach (*ta'eer*) rather than intrinsic impurity. He validates the profession by citing the Prophet’s (PBUH) practice of paying cuppers, arguing that if the work were forbidden, he would not have compensated them. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that common practice does not negate legal validity, provided the source of income is clean. Additionally, the Imam extends this ruling to the rental of a ram, reinforcing the concept that earnings from permissible assets are lawful regardless of societal stigma.
